Why fog nets catch less water than they used to

30 October 2026By Ada Rivers

On the ridge above the village, the fog nets have hung between their poles for thirty years, and for most of that time they filled the tanks below by noon. Lately, the keepers say, the tanks are half empty by the evening.

Ines Varga, who has mended the nets since she was a girl, first noticed it in a dry spring. The mesh looked the same, the fog came in as thick as ever, and yet the gauges at the foot of the ridge read lower every week.

Her notebook, kept in pencil and now in its fourth volume, records the water in each tank at dawn and dusk. It is, as far as anyone knows, the longest record of its kind, and the regional water board has started to copy it.

A finer mist

The first explanation the keepers reached for was the fog itself. Fog is made of droplets, and the size of the droplets decides how many of them strike a thread instead of flowing around it, the way sand catches on a sieve while flour passes through.

Measurements taken from the ridge, using a borrowed laser counter, suggest the droplets have become smaller over the last decade. Smaller droplets follow the air, curve around the threads and drift on, so a net of the same mesh catches fewer of them.

Why the droplets have shrunk is less clear. Cleaner air is one possibility, since fewer particles of dust and salt means fewer seeds for droplets to form on, and the ones that do form grow smaller, lighter and slower to settle.

Another is the wind, which on this ridge now blows a little faster at dawn, when most of the water is caught. A faster wind pushes more fog through the nets, but it also bends the mesh, and a bent net, the keepers say, sheds water before it reaches the gutter.

The nets themselves

Not everyone is convinced that the fog has changed. Tomas Brenner, an engineer who designed the newer nets on the eastern slope, thinks the problem lies in the mesh, which has aged in the sun and lost the fine fuzz that once held droplets in place.

He has tested strips of old and new mesh side by side in a wind tunnel, a narrow wooden box with a fan at one end and a kettle at the other. The new strips, he says, caught nearly a third more water than strips cut from the oldest nets on the ridge.

If he is right, the remedy is simple, if tiresome: replace the mesh every few years instead of mending it. The keepers, who like their old nets and the patches that tell their history, are not pleased by the idea, but they have agreed to try.

Three ways to help a fog net

1. Keep it taut: a slack net sways in the wind, and a swaying net throws its water off before the drops can gather, run down the threads and reach the gutter.

2. Keep it clean: dust, pollen and bird droppings clog the mesh, so a rinse with rainwater, never soap, every few weeks keeps the threads able to hold droplets.

3. Face it right: a net set square to the wind that brings the fog, not the strongest wind of the day, catches the most, so watch the fog before you set the poles.

4. Mind the gutter: a gutter that tilts the wrong way, or one blocked by leaves, loses more water than a torn net, and it is the cheapest part to fix, so check it first.

Varga, for her part, thinks both explanations may be true. The fog is finer, she says, and the nets are tired, and a finer fog on a tired net is the worst of both worlds, since the threads that might have held the smallest droplets are the ones worn smooth.

This winter the keepers will hang two new nets beside two old ones on the same stretch of ridge, and compare the water each one brings in over a full season. Brenner will bring his laser counter, and Varga will bring her notebook.

Whatever they find, the village will not go thirsty. The tanks still fill, if more slowly, and the old well at the bottom of the hill has never run dry, though nobody has had to draw from it in a generation.

Still, Varga says, it is strange to watch a net you know well catch less of a fog you know well. "You notice when an old friend goes quiet," she says. "You want to know why."
